title: Impact of Local Labor Demand Shocks on Wages

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy

**Method: Instrumental Variables (IV) using the Bartik shift-share instrument**

The research question asks how local labor demand shocks affect wages. OLS estimation of wages on local labor demand will be biased due to:
- **Simultaneity**: Wages and labor demand are jointly determined (labor supply responds to wages)
- **Omitted variables**: Unobserved local amenities, productivity shocks, or policies that affect both wages and labor demand

The **Bartik (shift-share) instrument** addresses this by constructing predicted labor demand changes from the interaction of pre-determined regional industry employment shares with national industry growth rates. This isolates the component of local labor demand variation driven by national trends rather than local conditions.

**Key assumptions:**
1. **Relevance**: The Bartik instrument is correlated with local labor demand (testable via first-stage F-statistic)
2. **Exclusion restriction**: National industry growth rates affect local wages *only* through their effect on local labor demand (conditional on controls)
3. **Exogeneity of shares/shocks**: Either the initial industry shares or the national growth rates (or their combination) are exogenous to local wage shocks — the modern "shift-share" literature (Goldsmith-Pinkham et al., 2020; Borusyak et al., 2022) formalizes these conditions

## 2. R Code

```r
# ============================================================
# Impact of Local Labor Demand Shocks on Wages — IV Analysis
# ============================================================

# Load required packages
if (!require("AER")) install.packages("AER", repos="https://cloud.r-project.org")
if (!require("lmtest")) install.packages("lmtest", repos="https://cloud.r-project.org")
if (!require("sandwich")) install.packages("sandwich", repos="https://cloud.r-project.org")

library(AER)
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# --- Read Data ---
df <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s83_data.csv")
cat("=== Dataset Overview ===\n")
cat("Dimensions:", nrow(df), "x", ncol(df), "\n\n")
str(df)
cat("\nSummary Statistics:\n")
print(summary(df))

# Check instrument variation
cat("\n=== Instrument (z) Distribution ===\n")
print(table(df$z))
cat("Proportion z=1:", mean(df$z), "\n\n")

# --- OLS Estimation (Naive) ---
cat("============================================\n")
cat("       OLS: Wages ~ Labor Demand + Controls \n")
cat("============================================\n")
ols <- lm(y ~ x + controls, data = df)
ols_robust <- coeftest(ols, vcov = vcovHC(ols, type = "HC1"))
print(ols_robust)
cat("\nOLS coefficient on x (labor demand):", coef(ols)["x"], "\n\n")

# --- First Stage: Labor Demand ~ Bartik Instrument ---
cat("============================================\n")
cat("       First Stage: x ~ z + controls        \n")
cat("============================================\n")
first_stage <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = df)
fs_robust <- coeftest(first_stage, vcov = vcovHC(first_stage, type = "HC1"))
print(fs_robust)

# First-stage F-statistic (robust)
fs_waldtest <- waldtest(first_stage, . ~ . - z, vcov = vcovHC(first_stage, type = "HC1"))
f_stat <- fs_waldtest$F[2]
cat("\nFirst-stage F-statistic (robust) on excluded instrument z:", round(f_stat, 2), "\n")
if (f_stat > 10) {
  cat("=> Instrument passes the Stock-Yogo weak instrument threshold (F > 10)\n\n")
} else {
  cat("=> WARNING: Potential weak instrument problem (F < 10)\n\n")
}

# --- IV / 2SLS Estimation ---
cat("============================================\n")
cat("  2SLS IV: Wages ~ Labor Demand + Controls  \n")
cat("  Instrument: Bartik shift-share (z)         \n")
cat("============================================\n")
iv <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = df)
iv_robust <- coeftest(iv, vcov = vcovHC(iv, type = "HC1"))
print(iv_robust)

iv_summary <- summary(iv, diagnostics = TRUE)
cat("\nIV Diagnostics:\n")
print(iv_summary$diagnostics)

cat("\n*** Key Result ***\n")
cat("IV coefficient on x (labor demand):", round(coef(iv)["x"], 4), "\n")
cat("Robust SE:", round(iv_robust["x", "Std. Error"], 4), "\n")
cat("t-statistic:", round(iv_robust["x", "t value"], 4), "\n")
cat("p-value:", format.pval(iv_robust["x", "Pr(>|t|)"], digits = 4), "\n\n")

# --- Comparison: OLS vs IV ---
cat("============================================\n")
cat("         OLS vs IV Comparison                \n")
cat("============================================\n")
cat("OLS coefficient on x:", round(coef(ols)["x"], 4), "\n")
cat("IV  coefficient on x:", round(coef(iv)["x"], 4), "\n")
cat("Difference (IV - OLS):", round(coef(iv)["x"] - coef(ols)["x"], 4), "\n\n")

# --- Robustness Check 1: IV without controls ---
cat("============================================\n")
cat("  Robustness 1: IV without controls          \n")
cat("============================================\n")
iv_nocontrols <- ivreg(y ~ x | z, data = df)
iv_nc_robust <- coeftest(iv_nocontrols, vcov = vcovHC(iv_nocontrols, type = "HC1"))
print(iv_nc_robust)
cat("IV coeff (no controls):", round(coef(iv_nocontrols)["x"], 4), "\n\n")

# --- Robustness Check 2: Reduced Form ---
cat("============================================\n")
cat("  Robustness 2: Reduced Form (y ~ z)         \n")
cat("============================================\n")
reduced_form <- lm(y ~ z + controls, data = df)
rf_robust <- coeftest(reduced_form, vcov = vcovHC(reduced_form, type = "HC1"))
print(rf_robust)
cat("\nReduced form coefficient on z:", round(coef(reduced_form)["z"], 4), "\n")
cat("Implied IV = RF/FS:", round(coef(reduced_form)["z"] / coef(first_stage)["z"], 4), "\n\n")

# --- Robustness Check 3: Hausman Test (OLS vs IV endogeneity) ---
cat("============================================\n")
cat("  Robustness 3: Durbin-Wu-Hausman Test       \n")
cat("============================================\n")
# Manual Hausman: include first-stage residuals in OLS
df$fs_resid <- residuals(first_stage)
hausman_reg <- lm(y ~ x + controls + fs_resid, data = df)
hausman_robust <- coeftest(hausman_reg, vcov = vcovHC(hausman_reg, type = "HC1"))
cat("Coefficient on first-stage residual (test of endogeneity):\n")
print(hausman_robust["fs_resid", ])
if (hausman_robust["fs_resid", "Pr(>|t|)"] < 0.05) {
  cat("=> x is endogenous at 5% level; IV is preferred over OLS\n\n")
} else {
  cat("=> Cannot reject exogeneity of x; OLS may be consistent\n\n")
}

# --- Robustness Check 4: Subsample analysis ---
cat("============================================\n")
cat("  Robustness 4: Split-sample stability       \n")
cat("============================================\n")
set.seed(42)
idx <- sample(1:nrow(df), nrow(df)/2)
iv_half1 <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = df[idx, ])
iv_half2 <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = df[-idx, ])
cat("IV coeff (subsample 1):", round(coef(iv_half1)["x"], 4), "\n")
cat("IV coeff (subsample 2):", round(coef(iv_half2)["x"], 4), "\n\n")

# --- Final Summary ---
cat("============================================\n")
cat("           FINAL SUMMARY                     \n")
cat("============================================\n")
cat("Causal effect of labor demand on wages (IV):", round(coef(iv)["x"], 4), "\n")
cat("95% CI: [", 
    round(coef(iv)["x"] - 1.96 * iv_robust["x", "Std. Error"], 4), ",",
    round(coef(iv)["x"] + 1.96 * iv_robust["x", "Std. Error"], 4), "]\n")
cat("First-stage F:", round(f_stat, 2), "\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings

**Expected sign and magnitude:**

1. **Positive IV coefficient**: A positive shift in local labor demand (driven by favorable national industry trends hitting regions with concentrated employment in those industries) should increase local wages. Standard labor economics predicts an upward-sloping labor demand curve in wage-employment space, so exogenous demand increases raise equilibrium wages.

2. **Magnitude**: Given the standardized/normalized nature of the data (variables appear roughly mean-zero with modest variance), I expect the IV coefficient to be positive, likely in the range of **0.3–0.8** — indicating that a one-unit increase in instrumented labor demand raises wages by 0.3–0.8 units.

3. **IV vs OLS comparison**: The IV estimate could be **larger than OLS** if there is attenuation bias from measurement error in local labor demand, or if simultaneity bias (higher wages reducing labor demand) attenuates the OLS coefficient toward zero. Alternatively, if omitted variables (e.g., local productivity) positively bias OLS, the IV estimate could be smaller.

4. **First-stage strength**: Since z is binary (0/1), the first stage essentially compares mean labor demand across z=0 and z=1 regions. I expect a significant first-stage relationship, though the binary nature of the instrument may yield a moderate F-statistic. If F > 10, the instrument is reasonably strong.

5. **Reduced form**: The Wald/IV estimator should be recoverable as the ratio of reduced-form to first-stage coefficients, providing a consistency check.

6. **Hausman test**: I expect some evidence of endogeneity of x, justifying the IV approach, though with only 300 observations and a binary instrument, precision may be limited.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Use Bartik shift-share as an instrument for local labor demand.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The analysis reveals a significant positive effect of local labor demand on wages.
